source.title: Scaling Laws for Behavioral Foundation Models over User Event Sequences

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures compute-optimal scaling in a new setting: behavioral models trained on user event sequences, using a feature-based embedder and transformer rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports other sweeps, including critical batch size, embedder share, depth, and negative-pool size. They are not included as rows unless they bear on a listed claim version. The absolute Stage 1 validation losses are not directly comparable across compute budgets because evaluation candidate pools differ; the paper says within-budget comparisons are apples-to-apples.
record.test_reason: The study fits compute-optimal allocation laws in a new behavioral event-sequence setting. Appendix D also fits power-law training-loss surfaces. It tests allocation and fitting dependence, but provides no comparable cross-budget held-out-loss curve or large-run loss prediction.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. More precisely, the parabolic validation-loss allocation has D/N decreasing from approximately 345 to 36, whereas the discrete grid winners are nonmonotonic. The authors also conclude that a roughly 2% embedder is optimal for their recipe, that metric choice changes practical training choices despite robust allocation exponents, and that negative sampling becomes memory-limited at the largest budget.
record.recipe_differences: This is a two-stage feature-based event-embedder and transformer setup trained on retail interaction sequences, with sampled-softmax objectives and batch-local or full-catalogue evaluation; it is not the language-model pretraining setup of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Allocation exponents and per-budget winners vary with evaluation metric; the per-budget training-loss-surrogate minima can differ from validation-loss minima. Batch-local and full-catalogue loss rankings can also disagree.

fits_no_version.finding: The same Stage 2 checkpoints have batch-local versus deployed-catalogue validation-loss rank correlation −0.95 at 10^19 FLOPs and batch size 512.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-based checkpoint rankings can reverse when evaluation candidate pools change in sampled-softmax behavioral models.

record.problems: The evidence is from one model stack and one anonymized retail interaction corpus. Stage 1 validation uses batch-local candidate pools, and absolute losses are not comparable across compute budgets. The study reports only a limited compute range and does not test other modalities or training regimes.
record.rows_left_out: The critical-batch-size, embedder-share, depth, and negative-sampling sweeps are not cataloged as separate rows because they do not directly measure the parameter/token compute-optimal allocation or the listed power-law loss claims. Depth was not tested at fixed parameter count.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out pretraining-loss scaling test. Behavioral Stage 1 absolute validation losses are not comparable across budgets.
No fit on small runs is validated by predicting loss on runs orders of magnitude larger.

Generality beyond one behavioral-model stack, corpus, training sequence length and four-decade compute range; independently measured token exponents; allocation under a common full-catalogue validation objective across budgets.
No architecture comparison holds total parameter count fixed across a wide range of depth and width.

Comparable held-out-loss power laws are not established. The additional loss fits concern a sampled training-loss surrogate; other modalities, transfer, fine-tuning and controlled repeated-data regimes are not tested.
No separate downstream-task performance scaling or predictive mapping from pretraining loss is evaluated. Next-event ranking metrics evaluate the training task itself.
No controlled comparison of corpora, training schedules or parameter-counting conventions explaining disagreements between published language-model laws.

missing.what: Training-loss power-law fits: Ltrain*(C)=2.485+1.50×10^3 C^-0.210 and Ltrain(N,D)=2.570+2.46×10^3/N^0.696+8.08×10^2/D^0.384, with RMSE 0.084 nats over 48 merged training points. Record these as sampled training-surrogate fits, not comparable held-out-loss evidence.

Parabolic validation-loss optima and their D/N series: approximately 345, 265, 222, 110, 36. These differ substantially from the discrete grid winners and are the points used for the headline allocation fit.

Discrete-versus-parabolic training-surrogate fitting comparison: discrete exponents 0.609±0.052 and 0.439±0.028 versus parabolic exponents 0.612±0.024 and 0.388±0.024; several per-budget parameter optima also shift. This directly measures fitting-choice dependence.
missing.locator: Appendix D, text surrounding Equations (10)–(13); Table 13

record.verdict_notes: V5 support comes from the overlooked training-loss equations, not from allocation exponents alone. Those equations do not establish a comparable held-out-loss law. Appendix D also inconsistently compares a 39.5M training parabolic optimum with a 19.4M validation grid winner at 10^18 FLOPs; Table 4 gives the validation parabolic optimum as 38.9M, so that passage cannot substantiate a large training-versus-validation parabolic-optimum difference.

versions.untested_parts: It does not establish held-out pretraining-loss power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute when other factors are not bottlenecks. Its held-out loss allocation analysis uses per-budget parabolic fits in log parameter count, and the paper cautions that absolute Stage 1 losses across budgets are not directly comparable.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of substantially larger runs.
The study tests a behavioral-model stack on one interaction corpus over 10^15–10^19 FLOPs; it does not test the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann allocation trend across language-model setups.
The depth sweep does not hold parameter count fixed while varying depth and width, and the width sweep does not vary hidden size at fixed depth.
It tests behavioral event-sequence modeling, not image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The ranking metrics are next-event evaluation metrics within the behavioral-model task, not downstream-task evaluations of language models or downstream performance predicted from language-model pretraining loss.

It reports sensitivity to evaluation metric and fitting/surrogate choices in this behavioral-model setup, but does not compare published language-model exponents across parameter-counting, schedule, or data choices.
